items.prompt: A tampered client POSTs to /api/attempts with an extra "correct": true and "score": 1 next to a wrong answer. What happens to those two fields?
items.answer: They are never copied: checkBody builds a fresh object from exactly itemId, response, timeSpent, mode and attempt, so the server re-grades and stores its own verdict
distractors: checkBody rejects the request with a 400 because unknown fields are forbidden
They are stored as the client's claim and later compared against the server grade
The server trusts them only when the response kind is self-graded
items.explanation: Dropping by construction (copy the allow-listed fields into a new object) means the client can submit an answer but can never claim a result.

items.prompt: Why does it matter that grade() reads no database, clock or window?
items.answer: Purity lets the same function run unchanged in the browser for instant feedback and on the server for the authoritative re-grade, so the two can never drift apart
distractors: Pure functions are memoized by React, so grading is computed only once per item
It lets the server skip re-grading whenever the client verdict arrives
It is needed so grade() can be called inside a database transaction
items.explanation: A grader that read Date.now(), the DB or window could not run in both places. One pure function serves the client, the route and the content checker.

items.prompt: gradeCode() uses options.runTests ?? runTests. What does this single optional parameter achieve?
items.answer: The server can inject the node:vm runner while grader.ts keeps no node: import, so it still bundles for the browser and tests can pass a fake runner
distractors: It lets the grader detect at runtime whether it is in Node or a browser
It allows learners to supply their own test runner with their submission
It makes code grading asynchronous so the API can stream results
items.explanation: Dependency injection at the smallest useful size: one optional parameter with a default keeps the grader pure and portable.

items.prompt: A multi-select item has 2 correct options out of 4. A learner ticks all 4. What score does gradeMulti give?
items.answer: 0 - two false positives cancel the two hits, and the net is floored at zero
distractors: 1 - both correct options were selected
0.5 - hits and misses are averaged across all four options
A negative score, so guessing everything is actively punished
items.explanation: Each wrong pick cancels one right pick and the net never goes negative, so selecting everything is never a winning strategy.

items.prompt: A learner gets an item right on the second try, but the client sends attempt: 1. Why can't the server catch this?
items.answer: The first miss on a retryable item is never posted, so the server has no record to check the attempt number against; it is a documented, accepted local-first risk
distractors: It can: the route looks up the previous attempt row and overrides the field
The grader detects second tries from the response shape and caps the score
attempt is ignored entirely; every success earns full credit regardless
items.explanation: attempt === 2 caps the score at 0.5, but only the client knows it was a second try. The route's Trust boundary comment names the hole and the fix (post the first miss).

items.prompt: timeSpent is clamped to 0..3600 seconds. How can a forged value still affect scheduling?
items.answer: Claiming a tiny time on a correct review of a card seen before makes ratingFor return Easy, pushing the next review further out
distractors: A huge value overflows the FSRS interval and schedules the card in the past
It cannot: the server measures time itself and ignores the client's number
A negative value is stored as-is and resets the card to New
items.explanation: Clamping bounds the range but not the meaning: timeSpent < budget * 0.5 with reps > 0 earns Easy. The route comment lists this as a known limit.

items.prompt: In the browser runner, a submission contains while (true) {}. What does the TIME_BUDGET_MS check do?
items.answer: Nothing - it runs only after the call returns, which never happens, so the tab hangs; the check only catches slow code that finishes
distractors: It interrupts the loop after 2 seconds and reports a timeout verdict
The browser's new Function compile step refuses infinite loops
It throws a TimeoutError from a setTimeout scheduled before the call
items.explanation: JavaScript cannot interrupt a synchronous function from the same thread. Preempting a runaway loop client-side needs a terminable Worker.

items.prompt: On the server the same infinite loop is graded through vmCompile. Why does it stop there?
items.answer: Each call runs via vm.Script runInContext with a timeout, which V8 enforces mid-loop and Node reports as ERR_SCRIPT_EXECUTION_TIMEOUT
distractors: The route runs grading in a worker thread that is terminated after 2 seconds
Next.js aborts any request handler that exceeds its response deadline
The vm context has no while keyword, so the code fails to compile
items.explanation: vm's timeout is enforced by V8 inside synchronous execution, so liveness is restored even though the code shares the server's thread.

items.prompt: A learner's solution calls arr.sort() on its input. Why can't that corrupt later test cases sharing the same array literal?
items.answer: runTests passes cloneArgs(tc.input), which structured-clones each argument before every call
distractors: Test inputs are frozen with Object.freeze, so sort() throws
Each test case is re-parsed from JSON storage right before it runs
The vm context copies arguments automatically on every call
items.explanation: Structured cloning isolates each test's inputs. Only uncloneable values (functions, objects holding functions) pass through as-is.

items.prompt: Why does seed() derive item ids as item-<authored id> instead of generating a UUID per run?
items.answer: So a re-seed upserts the same row and the learner's user_cards and attempts keep pointing at the item they were about
distractors: UUIDs are not supported as primary keys by better-sqlite3
Deterministic ids make the seed run faster because no randomness is needed
So that renaming an item id automatically migrates its history
items.explanation: The price is that an authored id becomes a permanent public key: a rename is seen as one removal plus one new item, and the new item starts with a fresh card.

items.prompt: The seeder upserts content rows with onConflictDoUpdate. Which strategy does it use for user_track_progress rows, and why?
items.answer: onConflictDoNothing - the row is created if missing and never overwritten, so a re-seed cannot reset a learner's level to 1
distractors: onConflictDoUpdate, so content edits to level thresholds reach every learner
DELETE then INSERT, so stale progress rows are cleaned up each run
They are not written by the seeder at all; the API creates them lazily
items.explanation: Content is a cache that may be refreshed freely; user state exists nowhere else, so the seeder only fills gaps in it.

items.prompt: An item disappears from the content files. What does the current seeder do with its database row?
items.answer: It sets is_published = 0 and keeps the row, because attempts and user_cards cascade on delete and a hard delete would erase the learner's history
distractors: It deletes the row; ON DELETE CASCADE then cleans up its attempts
It leaves the row published so existing cards keep being scheduled
It renames the row's id with a deleted- prefix to free the old id
items.explanation: Soft delete: unpublished items drop out of sessions and progress totals, and if the id returns the upsert republishes it with its history intact.

items.front: POST /api/attempts re-grades every answer (src/app/api/attempts/route.ts:114-126). Which two client inputs does it still take on faith, and why is that acceptable here?
items.back: attempt (whether this was the second try) and timeSpent (clamped, but a small value can turn Good into Easy). Reps is single-user and local, so a forged value only fools the person sending it; the fix for a multi-user version is to post the first miss and derive attempt server-side.

items.front: What does the node:vm runner in src/lib/executor.server.ts buy, and what does it explicitly not buy (lines 20-24)?
items.back: Liveness: an accidental infinite loop is stopped by a hard timeout instead of freezing the API. Not isolation: vm is not a security boundary, code can reach the host through prototype tricks. Fine for a local app running the learner's own code; remote code execution for any hosted multi-user version.

items.front: How does the generalised migrate() in src/lib/db/seed.ts:194-232 decide what to ALTER, and when does it refuse?
items.back: It builds SCHEMA_DDL in an in-memory database, compares each existing table's PRAGMA table_info with it, and ADDs any missing column with its NOT NULL and default. A missing primary key or NOT NULL column with no default cannot be added in place, so it throws and points at npm run db:reset. Additive only, idempotent, run before the DDL.

items.front: Why does the seeder DELETE an item's item_concepts rows and re-insert them (src/lib/db/seed.ts:397-404) instead of upserting each link?
items.back: An upsert can add a link but cannot express that a link is gone. Delete-then-insert for a small child collection is the simple correct way to make removals in content take effect.
